title: Faith for those who cannot study
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα προτρέπει ἐπὶ τὸ λόγῳ ἀκολουθοῦντας καὶ λογικῷ ὁδηγῷ παραδέχεσθαι δόγματα, ὡς πάντως ἀπάτης γινομένης τῷ μὴ οὕτω συγκατατιθεμένῳ τισί· καὶ ἐξομοιοῖ τοὺς ἀλόγως πιστεύοντας μητραγύρταις καὶ τερατοσκόποις, Μίθραις τε καὶ Σαβαδίοις. καὶ ὅτῳ τις προσέτυχεν, Ἑκάτης ἢ ἄλλης δαίμονος ἢ δαιμόνων φάσμασιν. ὡς γὰρ ἐν ἐκείνοις πολλάκις μοχθηροὶ ἄνθρωποι ἐπιβαίνοντες τῇ ἰδιωτείᾳ τῶν εὐεξαπατήτων ἄγουσιν αὐτοὺς ᾗ βούλονται, οὕτως φησὶ καὶ ἐν τοῖς Χριστιανοῖς γίνεσθαι. φησὶ δέ τινας μηδὲ βουλομένους διδόναι ἢ λαμβάνειν λόγον περὶ ὧν πιστεύουσι χρῆσθαι τῷ „μὴ ἐξέταζε ἀλλὰ πίστευσον“ καὶ „ἡ πίστις σου σώσει σε.“ καί φησιν αὐτοὺς λέγειν· „κακὸν ἡ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ σοφία ἀγαθὸν δ᾿ ἡ μωρία.“ λεκτέον δὲ πρὸς τοῦτο ὅτι εἰ μὲν οἷόν τε πάντας καταλιπόντας τὰ τοῦ βίου πράγματα σχολάζειν τῷ φιλοσοφεῖν, ἄλλην ὁδὸν οὐ μεταδιωκτέον οὐδενὶ ἢ ταύτην μόνην. εὑρεθήσεται γὰρ ἐν τῷ χριστιανισμῷ οὐκ ἐλάττων, ἵνα μὴ φορτικόν τι εἴπω, ἐξέτασις τῶν πεπιστευμένων καὶ διήγησις τῶν ἐν τοῖς προφήταις αἰνιγμάτων καὶ τῶν ἐν τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις παραβολῶν καὶ ἄλλων μυρίων συμβολικῶς γεγενημένων ἢ νενομοθετημένων. εἰ δὲ τοῦτ᾿ ἀμήχανον πῇ μὲν διὰ τὰς τοῦ βίου ἀνάγκας πῇ δὲ καὶ διὰ τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀσθένειαν, σφόδρα ὀλίγων ἐπὶ τὸν λόγον ᾀττόντων, ποία ἂν ἄλλη βελτίων μέθοδος πρὸς τὸ τοῖς πολλοῖς βοηθῆσαι εὑρεθείη τῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τοῖς ἔθνεσι παραδοθείσης; καὶ πυνθανόμεθά γε περὶ τοῦ πλήθους τῶν πιστευόντων, τὴν πολλὴν χύσιν τῆς κακίας ἀποθεμένων, ἐν ᾗ πρότερον ἐκαλινδοῦντο· πότερον βέλτιόν ἐστιν αὐτοῖς ἀλόγως πιστεύουσι κατεστάλθαι πως τὰ ἤθη καὶ ὠφελῆσθαι διὰ τὴν περὶ τῶν κολαζομένων ἐπὶ ἁμαρτίαις καὶ τιμωμένων ἐπὶ ἔργοις χρηστοῖς πίστιν, ἢ μὴ προσίεσθαι αὐτῶν τὴν ἐπιστροφὴν μετὰ ψιλῆς πίστεως, ἕως ἂν ἐπιδῶσιν ἑαυτοὺς ἐξετάσει λόγων; φανερῶς γὰρ οἱ πάντες παρ᾿ ἐλαχίστους οὐδὲ τοῦτο λήψονται, ὅπερ εἰλήφασιν ἐκ τοῦ ἁπλῶς πεπιστευκέναι, ἀλλὰ μενοῦσιν ἐν κακίστῳ βίῳ. εἴπερ οὖν ἄλλο τι κατασκευαστικόν ἐστι τοῦ τὸ φιλάνθρωπον τοῦ λόγου οὐκ ἀθεεὶ τῷ βίῳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπιδεδημηκέναι, καὶ τοῦτ᾿ αὐτοῖς συγκαταριθμητέον. ὁ γὰρ εὐλαβὴς οὐδὲ σωμάτων ἰατρὸν, πολλοὺς ἐπὶ τὸ βέλτιον νοσοῦντας ἀγαγόντα, οἰήσεται ἀθεεὶ πόλεσι καὶ ἔθνεσιν ἐπιδημεῖν· οὐδὲν γὰρ χρηστὸν ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἀθεεὶ γίνεται. εἰ δὲ ὁ πολλῶν σώματα θεραπεύσας ἢ ἐπὶ τὸ βέλτιον προαγαγὼν οὐκ ἀθεεὶ θεραπεύει, πόσῳ πλέον ὁ πολλῶν ψυχὰς θεραπεύσας καὶ ἐπιστρέψας καὶ βελτιώσας, καὶ ἀναρτήσας αὐτὰς θεοῦ τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι καὶ διδάξας πᾶσαν πρᾶξιν ἀναφέρειν ἐπὶ τὴν ἐκείνου ἀρέσκειαν καὶ πάντ᾿ ἐκκλίνειν, ὅσ᾿ ἀπάρεστά εἰσι θεῷ, μέχρι τοῦ ἐλαχίστου τῶν λεγομένων ἢ πραττομένων ἢ καὶ εἰς ἐνθύμησιν ἐρχομένων;
pass_a_gloss: After these things he (Celsus) urges (προτρέπει) [people] following reason (λόγῳ ἀκολουθοῦντας) and a rational guide (λογικῷ ὁδηγῷ) to accept doctrines (παραδέχεσθαι δόγματα), as deception (ἀπάτη) by all means arising for the one not assenting (συγκατατίθεσθαι) thus to certain things; and he likens (ἐξομοιοῖ) those believing irrationally (ἀλόγως πιστεύοντας) to begging priests of the Mother (μητραγύρται) and portent-watchers (τερατοσκόποι), to Mithrases and Sabaziuses (Μίθραι, Σαβάδιοι = devotees), and whatever one happened upon (προσέτυχεν), to apparitions (φάσματα) of Hecate or of another she-spirit (δαίμων, fem.) or of spirits. For as among those wicked men (μοχθηροί), stepping upon (ἐπιβαίνοντες) the simplicity/ignorance (ἰδιωτεία) of the easily deceived (εὐεξαπάτητοι), lead them where they wish, so he says it happens also among the Christians. He says some, not even wishing to give or receive an account (λόγον) about what they believe, use ‘do not examine (μὴ ἐξέταζε) but believe (πίστευσον)’ and ‘your faith (πίστις) will save (σώσει) you’. And he says they say: ‘evil (κακόν) is the wisdom in the world (ἡ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ σοφία), good (ἀγαθόν) the foolishness (μωρία).’ It must be said to this: if it were possible for all, having left the affairs of life (τὰ τοῦ βίου πράγματα), to have leisure for philosophising (σχολάζειν τῷ φιλοσοφεῖν), no one should pursue (μεταδιωκτέον) another road (ὁδόν) than this only. For there will be found in Christianity not less (that I may not say something vulgar/boastful, φορτικόν) examination (ἐξέτασις) of the things believed and explanation (διήγησις) of the riddles (αἰνίγματα) in the prophets and the parables (παραβολαί) in the gospels and of myriad other things done or legislated symbolically (συμβολικῶς). But if this is impossible, partly through the necessities (ἀνάγκαι) of life, partly through the weakness (ἀσθένεια) of men, very few rushing (ᾀττόντων) to reason/study (λόγος), what other better method (μέθοδος) for helping the many would be found than that handed down (παραδοθείσης) from Jesus to the nations (ἔθνη)? And we inquire about the multitude (πλῆθος) of believers, who put off (ἀποθεμένων) the great outpouring (χύσις) of wickedness (κακία) in which they formerly rolled (ἐκαλινδοῦντο): whether it is better for them, believing irrationally, to have been somehow restrained (κατεστάλθαι) in their ways (ἤθη) and helped through the belief about those punished (κολαζομένων) for sins (ἁμαρτίαι) and honoured (τιμωμένων) for good works (ἔργα χρηστά), or not to admit (προσίεσθαι) their turning (ἐπιστροφή) with bare faith (ψιλὴ πίστις) until they give themselves to examination of arguments. For plainly all except the fewest will not take even this which they have taken from simply having believed, but will remain in a worst life. If then something else is probative (κατασκευαστικόν) of the love-for-humankind of the Word (τὸ φιλάνθρωπον τοῦ λόγου) not without God (ἀθεεί) having sojourned (ἐπιδεδημηκέναι) in the life of men, this too must be counted along (συγκαταριθμητέον) with them. For the devout man (εὐλαβής) will not think that even a physician of bodies, having led many sick to the better, sojourns in cities and nations without God; for nothing good happens among men without God. And if the one having healed (θεραπεύσας) bodies of many or brought them forward to the better does not heal without God, how much more the one having healed and turned (ἐπιστρέψας) and bettered (βελτιώσας) souls of many, and having hung them upon (ἀναρτήσας) God over all (θεοῦ τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι), and having taught to refer every action to his pleasing (ἀρέσκεια) and to turn away from all things displeasing (ἀπάρεστα) to God, down to the least of things said or done or even coming into thought (ἐνθύμησις)?

pass_b_english: After this he urges people to accept doctrines by following reason and a rational guide, since anyone who assents to anything in another way is sure to be deceived. He likens those who believe without reason to the begging priests of the Great Mother and to readers of portents, to the devotees of Mithras and of Sabazius, and to whatever one happens to meet: the apparitions of Hecate, or of some other female spirit, or of spirits. For just as among these, wicked men often take advantage of the ignorance of the gullible and lead them wherever they wish, so, he says, it happens among the Christians too. He says that some, who are not even willing to give or to receive an account of what they believe, use the sayings “Do not examine, but believe” and “Your faith will save you” (Mark 5:34; Luke 7:50). And he says that they say: “Wisdom in the world is an evil thing, and foolishness a good one” (1 Corinthians 3:18–19).

To this we must reply that if it were possible for everyone to leave the business of life and devote themselves to philosophy, no one should follow any other way than this alone. For in Christianity there will be found, to say nothing more boastful, no less examination of what is believed, and explanation of the riddles in the prophets, of the parables in the Gospels, and of countless other things that happened or were laid down in the law as symbols. But if this is impossible, partly because of the necessities of life and partly because of human weakness, since very few press eagerly toward rational study, what better method of helping the many could be found than the one handed down to the nations by Jesus?

And we ask, concerning the multitude of believers who have put away the great flood of wickedness in which they once wallowed: is it better for them, believing without reason, to have had their ways somehow restrained, and to have been helped by their belief that people are punished for sins and honoured for good works? Or is it better to refuse their conversion on bare faith until they give themselves to the examination of arguments? For plainly all of them, apart from a very few, will not receive even what they have received from believing simply, but will remain in a most wicked life.

If, then, anything else serves to prove that the Word’s love for humankind has come into human life not without God, this too must be counted with those proofs. For a devout person will not suppose that even a physician of bodies, who has brought many of the sick to better health, visits cities and nations without God; for nothing good comes about among human beings without God. And if one who has healed the bodies of many, or brought them to better health, does not heal without God, how much more is this true of one who has healed, converted and bettered the souls of many, who has made them depend on God who is over all, and has taught them to refer every action to what pleases him and to shun everything displeasing to God, down to the least of the things said or done, or even entering the mind?

choices.choice: Celsus’s ‘Your faith will save you’ (ἡ πίστις σου σώσει σε) uses the future tense; the Gospel formula is the perfect ‘has saved you’ (Matthew 9:22; Mark 5:34; 10:52; Luke 7:50; 8:48; 17:19; 18:42), so the citation marks the Gospel saying Celsus echoes, not an exact quotation. ‘Wisdom in the world is an evil thing’ is Celsus’s distortion of 1 Corinthians 3:18–19, which Origen answers in chapter 13 (there Celsus’s wording is ‘in this life’, ἐν τῷ βίῳ). μητραγύρται = mendicant priests of the Great Mother (Cybele); Μίθραις τε καὶ Σαβαδίοις are plural personal names, rendered ‘devotees of Mithras and of Sabazius’. The dative construction ‘and whatever one happens upon, apparitions of Hecate…’ is loose in the Greek; rendered as it stands. ἄλλης δαίμονος is feminine: ‘some other female spirit’. τὸ φιλάνθρωπον τοῦ λόγου: λόγος could mean the Christian message, but the verb ἐπιδεδημηκέναι (Origen’s usual word for Christ’s coming) and the physician comparison point to the divine Word, so it is capitalised. Possible but uncertain allusions, not cited inline: ‘put away … wickedness’ (James 1:21) and ‘flood of wickedness’ (compare 1 Peter 4:4, ἀνάχυσις). φορτικόν rendered ‘to say nothing more boastful’.
‘urges us’ to ‘urges people’: the Greek names no object and Celsus speaks generally (Pass A has [people])
Hecate clause reordered so it reads as English; same content (ὅτῳ τις προσέτυχεν … φάσμασιν)
‘Plainly all of them’ to ‘For plainly all of them’ to keep γάρ
Scripture citations checked: Mark 5:34 and Luke 7:50 read ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε; 1 Corinthians 3:18–19 is the passage Celsus twists
